body: The good coat is the wrong thing to be kneeling in, but he came back for his keys, and at twenty to eight on a Sunday evening the hall is empty. A child was sick in the gents at about half four, during the second lot of tea, and somebody put paper towels over it and told somebody else, who told nobody. The caretaker does not come until Tuesday. So he is on his knees by the door with a bucket and a green cloth. When he has finished he stands in the car park for a minute working out whether the smell is on his hands or in his head, and then texts his wife to say he will be twenty minutes.

Nobody saw that and nobody will be told. He is the man who will preach in that hall at half past ten next Sunday, from the front, to about ninety people, and by then the floor will be dry and entirely unremarkable.

Foot washing survives as an occasional ceremony. It is performed once a year, generally by somebody senior, in front of a congregation, with clean feet and warm water, and everybody present understands it as a symbol of humility. Almost nobody is uncomfortable.

The original was not like that, and it is worth staying with the physical facts for a moment. People walked in open sandals on roads that carried animals, and everything on those roads ended up on their feet. Washing them was not a nice gesture at the door; it was the removal of ordure from between the toes of somebody you had invited to eat with you. Every household of any size had a settled answer to who did it, and the answer was never the host and never a guest. It was the job given to whoever in the household had the least standing. That is the whole content of the demonstration.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air today. One of the numbers already assigned is HM 387.50, Lead Like Yeshua — assigned and in build, not yet on air, with a Leader’s Hour at seven in the morning and Marketplace Mentorship at six in the evening written into its schedule and no audio on it yet.

So the demonstration only works if the person doing it had standing to lose. A servant washing feet is a Tuesday. A rabbi washing feet, in front of the men who had spent the afternoon arguing about which of them ranked highest, is a public inversion of the seating plan, and this is why Peter objects. He is not being squeamish about feet. He is being reordered, in company, and he can see precisely what it implies about every assumption he has been operating on since he met the man now kneeling in front of him.

It is difficult to hold on to that now because the language has been taken up and softened. Servant leadership is a phrase in management books, and mostly a good one; it has genuinely improved how a lot of organisations treat people. But once a thing becomes a leadership style it acquires an audience by definition. A style is something observed. The original was designed to be legible to the men in the room, certainly — but its content was the rank, not the watching, and a version that keeps the watching and drops the rank has kept the wrong half.

This band is arranged in a way that makes the same point in an unglamorous, structural key. Every station holds one frequency permanently, and no station holds a better sort of number than another. The flagship, the children’s station, the sleep frequency and the smallest language service on the dial hold their numbers on identical terms, and none can be moved to make room for something more popular. A number cannot be taken from a quiet station and given to a loud one, which means the arrangement cannot reward standing even where it would be convenient.
Set the ceremony beside the ordinary thing and see which of them the text is actually describing.

The annual ceremony is not fake, and it is not worth being clever about it. Congregations are genuinely moved by it and children who watch it remember it. It costs a senior man something real to kneel on a hard floor in front of people who work for him, and some of them go home and behave differently for a fortnight. What it cannot do is reach the part of the week where rank is actually administered. It is scheduled, so everyone arrives prepared. It is watched, so the humility is legible as humility. It is reciprocal, so nobody ends up with the worse end of it. And it finishes: the ordinary distribution of unpleasant jobs resumes on Monday, untouched, and everybody has been to a service about it.
The test of the thing is whether it survives nobody finding out.

A woman of fifty-four lets herself into a primary school at ten past seven on a Monday in February. She has been the head for nine years. She puts the heating on, puts the chairs down off the tables in four classrooms, and mops the entrance where the rain has come under the door over the weekend. The caretaker’s wife started treatment in January and he does not come in until nine now. At twenty to eight she goes to her office and does emails with her coat on, because the building has not warmed up. Staff arrive from eight and the school is ready, and nobody remarks on it, because there is nothing to say about a school being ready. She has done this since half term.

Everybody in that building knows the head does not put out chairs. That is not incidental to what happened; it is the content of it, and it is why she cannot tell anyone. The moment it is mentioned it becomes a different act.

The honest cost is real and should not be smoothed over. Unwitnessed service is thankless by construction, and thankless work curdles. People who do it for long enough often end up quietly keeping a ledger, and the ledger poisons them, and they are then twice as difficult to help because nobody knows there is anything to help with. It does not scale, and it is regularly exploited by people who notice a job is being covered and never ask by whom.

But the resentment is not a flaw in the practice. It is the instrument, and it is the only honest one available. If a task performed where nobody can see it starts to sour within a week, that is accurate information about what a person believes concerning their own standing, and no amount of teaching would have produced it. This is the diagnostic the ceremony cannot run, because the ceremony has an audience, and an audience pays you in the same currency you were about to give up.

So the question the passage puts is narrower and harder than the one the ceremony asks. It is not whether you would kneel with a towel while the congregation watched. It is what you do about the job your position is understood to exempt you from, on an ordinary Monday, when nobody will be told and no credit will attach. Rank is administered in small allocations all week. That is where the inversion has to happen or it does not happen.
All of which is argument, and argument stays theory until something is actually playing.

Four kinds of programming run on this dial and it is worth knowing they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns, and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God aloud. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 361.90, Jubilee Kids Party. That will look like an odd recommendation in an essay about rank until you consider where rank is actually visible in a household, which is in who decides what is playing. The adult chooses. The adult has always chosen. Putting the children’s frequency on in the car when you are the one driving, and leaving it on, and not sighing at the third song, is a small and completely unwitnessed inversion of exactly the kind this article has been describing. It carries family-celebratory programming, a Party Morning at eight and an After-School Bash at four, and it is not aimed at you. That is the point of recommending it.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it nearer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

Take that as an invitation rather than a challenge. Put HM 361.90 on in the car this week on a journey you are driving, for children who did not ask for it, and leave it running the whole way. Nobody will know you did, which is the only condition that makes it worth anything. If it irritates you by the second song, that is not the station failing. That is the instrument working, and it is telling you something true about what you think your position exempts you from.
